limbs.1_configuredWithoutADeliverableSender: describeAlertConfiguration() returns configured:true, channel:'email' on OPERATIONAL_ALERT_EMAIL and RESEND_API_KEY alone, while dispatchOperationalAlert() sends from PASSWORD_RESET_FROM_EMAIL || 'alerts@safety-insite.invalid'. The .invalid TLD is reserved by RFC 2606 and can never be a verified Resend sending domain, so with only those two variables every send is rejected while /health/ready reports the channel configured.
limbs.2_deliveryResultDiscarded: Both branches are void fetch(...).catch(() => undefined) with no logging of a non-2xx response. Not throwing is correct and matches the §287 audit-write rule. Not recording is not: an unverified domain, a revoked key or a suspended account produces no signal inside the product.
limbs.3_emailBranchNeverExecuted: The §291 and §292 alert proofs both ran against a local HTTP webhook receiver. OPERATIONAL_ALERT appears in exactly three files — the dispatcher, the health controller and the register — so no committed test or script sets it. The channel the owner selected at §293 has zero executed coverage.

MO_2.consequenceIfSection293HadProceeded: Setting the two variables the register named would have flipped /health/ready from an honest NOT_CONFIGURED to alerting: configured over a channel that delivers nothing — a false green about monitoring, which is worse than the red it replaces and directly inverts the §291 guarantee that 'nothing is watching' is a visible fact rather than a silent assumption.
MO_2.whyNotAThresholdBBlocker: Closing MO-1 by proving ACTUAL RECEIPT inherently demonstrates a deliverable sender is configured, so MO-2 does not stand between the owner and Threshold B. Registering it as a B blocker would inflate a latent-configuration risk into an owner action, and there is no owner action in it: every limb is engineering work.
